Many founders I know carry that fear:

You spend years building.
You finally find traction.
Then one of the giants ships your roadmap as a free feature, and your valuation halves before lunch.

Push prompts, instructions, and data through the same connection.

34 minutes condensed into 60 seconds.
What did I miss?

Sold AutoDS to @[urn:li:organization:861427|Fiverr] at 28.
Turning 31 today got me reflecting on what actually got me there:

1. Pick your co-founder like your spouse. You'll see them more.
2. Kill the side projects. Focus is the only real edge.
3. Be lazy. If a task repeats, automate it.
4. Make mistakes fast. Be professional, not perfect.
5. Hire HR before you think you need it. Culture doesn't scale by accident.
6. Skip the business plan, but stay close to the data.
7. Don't wait for the perfect product. Ship before it's ready.
8. Be home for dinner. The work will be there in the morning.
9. Enjoy the ride. Real success comes from loving the work.
10. Treat it like a game. The day it stops being fun, you're playing the wrong one.

Took me years to learn. Hope it saves you some (:

One simple idea completely changed the way I run my company-

Treat yourself like a product.

You spend weeks on your product roadmap, but when it comes to your own growth?
Bottom of the list.

The truth? It isn't simple.

Pushing at 200% to win a market is one thing.
The real challenge is building a life that doesn't collapse while you do it.

Three things that help me stay on the list:

1. Personal OKRs: I roadmap my health and growth exactly like a new feature.
Exercises and learning time are defined and scheduled.

2. Prioritize: No matter what’s on my desk, I’m home for dinner with my wife.

3. Buying Shortcuts: Just as I hire experts in business to move faster, I hired a personal coach to shorten my learning curve and fix my own bugs.

You'd never ship a product without a roadmap, testing, and iteration.

Why run yourself without one?

Tired of re-explaining who you are to every new AI chat?
Here's the one problem with AI: People can smell it.

But what if your AI wrote exactly like you?

The fix is a Master Prompt. One doc. 

Pasted into every new chat.
ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok.

Here's how to build yours:

1. Write your IDENTITY.
☑ What you do, for whom, with what outcome.
☑ The one problem your people lose sleep over.
☑ What makes your approach different? Skip "I care", everyone does.

2. Write your MINDSET.
☑ The 3 beliefs you'd defend at a dinner table argument.
☑ How you actually decide. Data first? Gut first? Frameworks first?
☑ What winning looks like for the people you serve.

3. Write your VOICE.
☑ Describe yourself as a friend would. ("The cousin who makes hard stuff simple.")
☑ Paste 5 real sentences you've already written.

4. Write your GUARDRAILS.
☑ 3 things your voice is NOT. ("Not corporate. Not preachy. Not desperate.")
☑ Banned words. The buzzwords that make you cringe.

5. Test it, then port it everywhere.
☑ Open a fresh chat. Paste the doc. Ask the AI to write something only you would write.
If the output sounds like you, ship it.
If it doesn't, find the missing layer and add detail.
☑ Save the file. Paste it as the first message in every new chat.

6. Update it after every conversation.
☑ You evolve. The doc should too. Add new beliefs and achievements. 
☑ End every chat with three commands: "Save what we talked about. Update the master prompt. Tell me what changed."

Now the output reads like your writing.
Because every layer is built on what's already yours.

(Save this to duplicate yourself into any AI.)

@[urn:li:organization:74126343|Anthropic]'s team just dropped the workflow trick they use internally.
If you're in the "approve all without reading" gang, here's the shift you need to take-

MD files → HTML.

Tested it last week.
45 design screens reviewed in one afternoon.

How to start:
1. Tell Claude: “Make it an HTML file.”
That's it.

And if you want to level up:

2. Add comment fields right on the page, so you can approve and request changes directly on what you see.

"Build me an HTML page for [your content], with Approve/Changes buttons and comment fields on each item. Save notes to a local file."

3. When done leaving notes, write: "Fix the notes." The agent reads every comment, applies the fixes, and ships the next version.

The human brain isn't built to process walls of plain text. We need color, layout, and visual hierarchy that we can scan at a glance.

A visual surface means reviewing at the speed at which the brain runs. And it is much more fun.

My company was making millions, but I had zero in my bank account.

For the first 5 years of AutoDS, I didn't take a salary.
Every dollar went back into the business.
"This is what it takes," I told myself.

I was wrong.

Setting your own salary is a founder's mental trap:

- Take too much: You look like a lifestyle founder. 
- Take too little: You work your ass off, but can’t cover rent. It's hard to keep up in the long run.

9 years in, here’s my rule for every first-time founder: Pay yourself enough to think straight.
Enough to move money stress into the background.

When you’re in survival mode, your judgment is the first thing to go.

If you’re worried about your personal bank account, you’ll make desperate decisions for your company’s bank account.

Founders, how did you find your sweet spot number?

If you're building with agents in 2026, you know how fast things are going.

I spent yesterday at @[urn:li:organization:96691066|LangTalks] AI Engineering Conference, and here are the shifts I walked away with:

1. Prompts stopped being the focus.

We are in a new era.
Nobody on stage talked about prompting. They talked about the system around the agent: tracing, wiring, feedback loops. 

Writing a prompt is the easy part.
The actual job is to ensure the prompt works the same way on day 30 as on day 1.

2. The bugs got much harder to find.

The output looks fine in every spot check.
Then you open the dashboard and realize something has been off for a month.
No crash, no error, just a quiet decline.

Monitoring AI stopped being debugging. It became observation.

3. Gamification for agents is the next big hit.

Not every builder wants to live inside a black terminal.
Different people, different work styles, and tools should reflect that.

The standout demo was AgentCraft by @[urn:li:person:dNjRKYlJI-|Ido Salomon]. A Warcraft-style platform that turns AI agents into units on a map, making human-AI collaboration something you can actually see.

This is exactly how I think about work. Business is a game.

The field grew up. Less hype, more execution.
Which shift hits you hardest?

Thanks to @[urn:li:person:YPoSABXrTQ|Gal Peretz] and @[urn:li:person:yYkemo0Xsg|Lee Twito] for the production, and to all the AI agents in the audience, who probably implemented the talks before I left the building (:

We built a software that actually worked.
The only problem?

Nobody gave a damn.

So I did the logical thing: I flew across the world to buy a 20-year-old influencer a coffee.

We set the meeting in a coffee shop in Manhattan.

I sat there for an hour.
Checking my phone 40 times.

He didn't show up.

I wanted to flip a table, but settled for aggressively refreshing my Gmail instead.

I walked back to the hotel, feeling like an absolute idiot.

On the flight back to Tel Aviv, I was just pissed off.

I decided right there: I'd never let one stranger be the bottleneck between our customers and us again.

We'd build our own channel.

So we went all in.
100 videos in 100 days.

At first? Crickets.
It felt like shouting into a completely empty room.

But then the algorithm caught up.
Today, the @[urn:li:organization:11699535|AutoDS - Automatic Dropshipping Tools] YouTube channel has 397K subscribers.

I still don't know what that influencer is doing today.
But if I had just flown home and accepted defeat, we'd still be at the mercy of someone else's calendar.

The coffee is much better in Tel Aviv anyway.

How does the worst mistake of your career become a personal brand win?

@[urn:li:person:cI3V8REYJT|Jeremy Crane], The CEO of @[urn:li:organization:68890068|PocketOS], just gave a masterclass in building in public when it breaks.

Here's the story:

An AI agent at PocketOS did something no one asked it to do.

In 9 seconds, the production database was deleted. Backups too.

3 months of customer data vanished.

The rules were in the system prompt.
It violated every one.

Was it the team's fault? Absolutely.

But...

Most founders in this situation would have hidden in their Slack DMs and quietly rebuilt the company.

Crane did the opposite.

He posted a long, public breakdown on X that went viral.

His authority only grew from there.

Here's what everyone running AI can learn from this:

1. Minimum permissions only.
Separate tokens for staging and production.

2. Backups off-service.
If your AI can delete the data, it shouldn't be able to delete the backup.

3. Post your failures. Take ownership.
They can build more brand than any win.

Years ago, hackers broke into AutoDS and changed every customer's username overnight.

I went live on Facebook the same day.
Walked everyone through what happened, why, and what we were doing to prevent it.

Zero customers left.

Real brands aren't built when everything works.
They're built on what breaks.

For the past few weeks, I've been using something that changed how I work with Claude-

It's called find-skills.
A skill that finds other skills.

1. You describe your problem.
2. It scans the open-source skill libraries.
3. Pulls the ones that fit.
4. Then you tell Claude to plug them into your workflow.

The first time I used it, I asked for something simple:

"I need an agent that does QA on my code."

It found four different skills for that job.
I told Claude to learn from all of them.
Built me one super agent.

But here's what I didn't expect.

Claude didn't just give me answers.
It asked me the right questions about my code before I shipped it.

The questions sharpened what I was trying to build before I wrote a single line.

That's the part most people miss.

Every AI group I'm in, someone is asking, "How do I do X with Claude?"

Wrong forum.
Just ask Claude.

Link to the find-skills repo in the first comment.

I hiked a mountain in shorts at -15°C.

Here's what 5 days with @[urn:li:person:1_CTy7ANzz|Wim Hof] taught me:

1. The first step is the hardest.
The hard part of the mountain wasn't the top - it was the bottom.

Taking the first step into the snow.
The first dip in the frozen lake.

The beginning is where the resistance lives.

2. Our body knows things the mind doesn't.
After every session, I was frozen solid.

I couldn't move my fingers.
I couldn't move my toes.

At the top of the mountain, I ordered a hot chocolate and couldn't even hold the cup.

Then I started breathing the way they taught us.
Slow. 
Deep. 
Deliberate.

I sent warm thoughts to my hands and feet.
My fingers were working again within a minute.

3. If it scares me, that's the sign to do it.
@[urn:li:person:qjUxMYsDbW|Amit Giladi] told me over coffee that it was the best wellness event he'd ever joined.

I didn't know where I was going.
I didn't know the plan.
It scared me.
So I booked the ticket.

Now I'm passing it on.

Don't think about it. 
Just go.

The most expensive lie I told myself for 5 years:

"Reinvesting EVERY dollar is the growth strategy."

In the first 5 years of AutoDS, I didn't take a salary.

Zero.

100% of profits went back in.

I stopped opening my personal bank app.
There was nothing to check.
The company number was the only number that mattered.

That's what founders do, I told myself.

The spreadsheet was healthy.
The operator wasn't.

At that moment, I realized I needed to make a change.
I need to start treating myself the same way I treat the product.

Here's what that looks like in practice:

1. I roadmap my growth.

Every quarter, I set personal goals the same way I set product OKRs.
What skill am I building? What habit am I fixing? If it's not on my calendar, it doesn't exist.

2. I debug myself first.

When my focus drops, I don't push harder.
I check the basics.
Sleep. Food. Exercise.
Most performance problems aren't motivation problems. They're infrastructure problems.

3. I delegate ruthlessly.

If someone can do it 70% as well as I, they're doing it.
I stopped editing decks, reviewing minor expenses, and scheduling my own meetings a long time ago. That freed up hours.

You wouldn't ship a product without a roadmap, testing, and iteration.

The operator deserves the same.

I set up AI agents to replace my entire team.

Including me.

And let them run.

For 2 weeks, I've been using one of the most viral AI tools.

Paperclip.
An open-source tool that lets you hire AI agents.

You sit on the board.
They run the company.

Day one, I was hooked.

I set a goal for my CEO agent.
He broke it into tasks, hired a CTO, CTO hired engineers.
They started building.

The dashboard tracked every agent, every dollar, every task.
It looked like a real company.
Until I checked the output.

What came back was a blurry copy of a blurry copy of what I originally asked for.
Same as the telephone game.

I told the CEO what I wanted.
CEO told CTO.
CTO told the engineer.
Every handoff dropped context.

Real people push back.
Agents don't. They just execute the drift.

AI can do everything except apply your judgment.
You still have to encode that yourself.

Paperclip is a great tool for managing AI agents.
But the "zero human company" story? Marketing.
Humans aren't going anywhere.

Is this not the greatest time in history to be building?

I spent the first 5 years at AutoDS doing almost everything myself.
Today I barely touch a task list.

Here's the one rule that freed 80% of my time.

The 70% rule: if someone can do the task at least 70% as well as you, they're doing it.

Not 100%.
Not 90%.
70%.

Sounds risky.
But here's what happened when I applied it:

First hire took YouTube off my plate.
Then finance.
Then product ops.

One by one, every task that passed the 70% test became someone else's job.

The result?
Scaled to 1M+ paying users and sold AutoDS to @[urn:li:organization:861427|Fiverr].

I broke the full framework down slide by slide.
The 70% rule that changed everything 👇

@[urn:li:organization:11699535|AutoDS - Automatic Dropshipping Tools]

We went from one brand to five.
Same marketing team. Not a single hire added.

And we're not the only ones:
→ @[urn:li:organization:74126343|Anthropic] built a $60B company with one person (!) running growth marketing.
→ @[urn:li:organization:105614038|Cursor] scaled to $2B in revenue. Zero traditional marketing spend.
→ @[urn:li:organization:30898036|Notion] hit 20M+ users. Nearly all organic.

Here's how we do it.
I call it the 10-80-10 rule:

10% - we ideate. Brand voice, audience, strategy.
80% - AI executes. Content, funnels, designs, campaigns.
10% - we review, sniff test, ship.

The human brings taste and vision.
AI does the heavy lifting you shouldn't be doing twice.

This is what marketing in 2026 actually looks like. 
Not "AI is coming for your job" think pieces.
Just a team that quietly scaled 5x.

What's the one task AI cut from hours to minutes for you?

2 people team built a $1.8B company.
But it’s not as shiny as it sounds.
Here’s the story:

Matthew Gallagher started Medvi from his living room in LA. 
$20K. Two months. 
An online telehealth company selling weight loss prescriptions.

His tech stack?
ChatGPT, Claude, Grok for code. 
MidJourney and Runway for ads. 
AI agents for customer service.

First year - $401 million in revenue.
$65 million in profit.

His only hire? His brother.

For comparison, Hims & Hers generates similar revenue with 2,400 employees and 5.5% margins. 
This guy runs at 30%+.

Sounds like a dream.

But here’s what he actually built-
A marketing layer on top of real companies that employ the doctors, ship the medication, and write the prescriptions.

A middleman.
A very fast, AI-powered middleman.

Now here’s where it gets ugly:
- The FDA flagged them for misbranding.
- 5,000+ ads running with doctors that don't exist.
- A lawsuit claiming the product doesn't even work.

I've been in e-commerce for 16 years. 
I've seen this pattern before - someone finds a hot market, moves fast, and cashes out before the window closes.

The tools changed.
The playbook didn't.

AI made it possible to build a billion-dollar business with two people.
That's the trend. And it's just getting started.

Some will build real value.
Some will scam at scale.

The technology doesn't care which one you choose.

I filmed 300+ videos for AutoDS.
Sweaty palms every time.

But here's the thing - AutoDS YouTube got us millions in revenue.

Not because the videos were perfect.
Because my face was in them.

People follow people, not logos:
- @[urn:li:organization:15564|Tesla]: 30M followers vs. Elon Musk: 187M
- @[urn:li:organization:108171|Spanx]: 400K followers vs. @[urn:li:person:5dsORmkQ1i|Sara Blakely]: 2M
- @[urn:li:organization:8028|Virgin]: 700K followers vs. @[urn:li:person:NZzthVIrp9|Richard Branson]: 15M

I get it though.
"I look weird on camera."
"Who am I to post this?"
"What will people think?"

I pressed publish before I could think twice.

3 things that made it possible:

1. I only filmed. Editing, captions, posting - someone else handled all of it.
Separating "being the face" from "running the machine" was the biggest unlock.

2. I accepted the cost of entry. Your first 10 videos will be bad.
That's not failure, that's the process.
The only person replaying your video in their head is you.

3. I batched everything. One filming day = 10 videos = a full month of content.
Your phone + your story is the highest-converting setup you'll ever have.

The hardest part isn't the editing or the algorithm.
It's pressing record.

Block one hour this week.
Film one 30-second video.

What's actually stopping you?

3 employees quit AutoDS in the last 6 months.
I'm writing this with a smile.

They didn't leave because they were unhappy.
Not because they found something better.

They left because they started their own business.

When they came to tell me, I only had one thing to say-

Good luck.
And I truly meant it.

When I started AutoDS, I couldn't imagine it would become not only a successful company, but a school of entrepreneurship for our own team.

I once heard a joke that suddenly feels relevant:
"Cigarette companies kill their best customers. Condom companies kill their future customers."

AutoDS? Sometimes we grow people so well that they leave to chase their own dreams.

That's either the worst retention strategy in history or the best proof that the culture actually works.

I'll take it.

@[urn:li:organization:11699535|AutoDS - Automatic Dropshipping Tools]

No team. No code. Just a conversation with an agent.
I just spent 3 hours listening to the man behind one of the most controversial open-source AI projects, @[urn:li:person:6KvxLvpY1J|🦄 Peter Steinberger], who built @[urn:li:organization:111321012|OpenClaw] and broke GitHub records.

Here's what stayed with me:

1. Peter sent a voice message to his agent on WhatsApp by accident. The agent had no voice support. So it figured out how to convert the audio, transcribe it, and reply on its own. He never taught it how to do any of that.

2. He wrote a personal file for his agent - who he is, how he thinks, what matters to him. The agent started adapting on its own. After Peter had shoulder surgery, the agent sent him a message in the hospital asking if he was okay. Peter never told it about the surgery. It just knew.

3. Peter watched his own agent click the "I'm not a bot" checkbox on his screen. A bot, proving it's not a bot. And it passed.
We're only getting started.

If you're building with AI agents, here's what to take from this:

- Treat them like junior employees, not tools.
- Stop over-instructing. The WhatsApp story happened because Peter didn't limit what the agent could try. Give it a goal, not a script.
- Keep your prompts short. The best builders go through a phase of over-engineering everything. They come back to simple and direct.

3 hours condensed into 2 minutes.
What did I miss?

You love tech. You really do.
But somewhere between the 4th AI tool launch this week and your actual to-do list, you stopped keeping up.

You're not alone.

Most people genuinely care about staying ahead, but when it comes to getting work done, there's just no bandwidth left to evaluate every new tool that drops.

So they do one of two things:
try everything and burn out, or ignore everything and fall behind.

Here's what I do to stay sharp without drowning in noise:

1. Start from the need, then look for a solution.
Stop chasing trends and focus on what's actually slowing you down.

2. Pick 2-3 people you trust. Ignore the rest.
I follow a handful of people who actually test what they recommend. That's it.
Find your trusted sources and cut out everything else.

3. The tool that works is always better than the tool that's trending.
8 months ago, we automated a reporting workflow, saving us 6 hours a week.
Last month, a better tool was launched.
Did we switch? No.
Once a quarter, we review the tool we use and decide if anything needs to change.

You don't need to try every tool. 
You need a system for deciding which ones are worth your time.

I met him at a coffee shop. He was leaning in, eyes glowing, showing me his screen with pure excitement.

He walked me through every feature.

The product was impressive. No doubt.

Then I asked the only question that matters: "How many customers have paid for this?"

The silence told me everything. 

Zero.


My heart broke for him. 

How was I supposed to tell this guy that he’s been sprinting in the wrong direction?


I’m writing this now so fewer hearts (and bank accounts) break:

If they aren't trying to hand you money for a product that doesn't exist yet, don't build it.
Don't write a single line of code.

Instead- 

1. Find a painful problem.
2. Build a landing page with a price tag.
3. If they don't buy, pivot.

Sell the vision until the market literally forces you to build the solution.
